THE PRODUCT PROPOSAL

Buy for when
you’ll cook.

A customer planning tomorrow’s dinner needs to know whether the pack they receive will support that meal.

What I observed

On the public Licious wings page I reviewed, the product description gives a general four-day shelf-life instruction. I did not see a minimum remaining life at delivery or a promise covering a chosen cooking time.

Reviewed product page ↗ · Public view reviewed 7 November 2026. This is an observed gap in that view, not evidence of unsafe handling. The signed-in app and checkout remain unverified.

What changes for the customer?

OBSERVED PUBLIC VIEW

General shelf-life guidance

The reviewed description provides a shelf-life instruction, without a visible promise for the customer’s intended meal.

“Will the pack I receive cover tomorrow’s dinner?”
PROPOSED EXPERIENCE

A promise matched to the meal

The customer’s cooking time determines which products, delivery slots and batches are eligible.

“This delivery option can support your selected mealtime.”

A delivery slot answers when it arrives.
The proposed promise covers the usable life remaining for the intended meal.

The proposed flow

  1. Choose when to cook. Tonight, tomorrow, or a selected cooking time.
  2. See eligible choices. Show products and delivery slots that can meet that requirement.
  3. Allocate an eligible batch. Use actual expiry, release and quality information under approved storage rules.
  4. Recheck before dispatch. If the promise changes, explain it and offer an explicit choice to the customer.
For example: cooking tomorrow at 7 p.m.

If the batch available for an early delivery cannot cover that meal, offer a later delivery with an eligible batch. The earlier-dated stock can still serve customers cooking sooner, where approved rules allow.

Try this scenario in the demo ↗

Why this could create value

Conversion

Give planned-meal buyers confidence to purchase by answering their freshness question before checkout.

Inventory efficiency

Match earlier-dated eligible stock with customers cooking sooner, preserving later-dated stock for later meals.

Repeat purchasing

Make freshness a useful, verifiable part of the buying experience that customers can return for.

These are hypotheses to test. The prototype establishes no revenue uplift or reduction in waste.

The commercial test

First confirm planned-meal demand, current app capabilities and reliable batch data. Then run a bounded pilot: measure delivered-order conversion and repeat purchasing alongside contribution after extra picking constraints, fulfillment costs, waste, refunds and guarantee costs.

Reject the idea if customers mostly cook immediately, the capability already exists, or the added costs erase the benefit.

What is already built

A working customer-flow prototype and Java 21 reference API demonstrate cooking-time eligibility, alternate delivery slots, earliest eligible batch selection, expiring stock holds and rejection after a batch’s quality status changes. The reference also covers concurrent reservations, idempotent retries and quote/cart binding.

The hosted demo runs a browser reference model. The downloadable source runs the Java API locally. All inventory and policy parameters are simulated. The prototype rechecks at acceptance; production dispatch checks would require fulfillment integration and approved operating rules.
